questions.stem: A procurement coordinator uploads a 40-page supplier agreement and asks Claude for a one-page summary for the purchasing manager, who must decide whether to renew. Every statement in the summary checks out against the contract. Then a colleague points out that the agreement has an auto-renewal clause with a 90-day notice window, and the summary never mentions it. Before sending, what is the MOST reliable way to check that the summary is complete?

options.text: Ask Claude in the same conversation whether its summary left anything important out, and add whatever it lists before sending.
Check the summary against what a renewal decision depends on: term, renewal and notice, price changes, termination, liability.
Regenerate the summary and ask for more detail, since a longer summary is less likely to skip important clauses in the agreement.
Add the auto-renewal clause the colleague found and send it, since every other statement was already verified as accurate.

questions.explanation: Accurate and complete are two different checks. Every sentence in this summary is true, but it still leaves out the clause that matters most for a renewal decision. Completeness has to be judged against **what the reader needs to decide**. Write down the points a renewal decision depends on, then confirm each one in the source contract and in the summary. That turns a vague read-through into a targeted check, and it catches the gap the colleague found as well as any others nobody has noticed yet.

whyWrong.A: Asking Claude to review its own summary produces more model output, not evidence. It may say nothing is missing, or list items without checking them against the contract. You still have to go to the source.
whyWrong.C: A longer summary is not a more complete one. It can still skip the clause that matters, and the extra length makes it harder for the manager to read and for you to check.
whyWrong.D: This fixes the one gap someone happened to spot. The fact that a key clause was missed at all suggests others could be missing too, and nothing systematic has been checked.

questions.mindset: Accurate is not the same as complete; check the output against what the reader needs to decide.

questions.stem: In one message, an HR coordinator asks Claude for a welcome email to a new hire that (1) confirms the start date, (2) lists what to bring on day one, (3) explains parking and (4) names the onboarding buddy. The draft is warm and polished. What is the BEST first step in checking it before sending?

options.text: Read it for tone and grammar, since a draft this polished usually covers everything that was asked for.
Ask Claude to confirm that the draft followed every instruction in the original request before sending.
Paste the draft into a fresh conversation and ask Claude to rate its overall quality on a scale from 1 to 10.
Reopen the request, tick off each of the four items in the draft, and check that each detail is correct.

questions.explanation: The simplest completeness check is to compare the output with the request **item by item**. Multi-part requests are where a requirement most often gets dropped or blurred. Ticking off each item against the draft shows whether all four are present, and checking the details (the actual date, the buddy's name) shows whether they are right.

whyWrong.A: Good writing says nothing about completeness. A fluent, well-structured email can still leave out the parking information or get the start date wrong.
whyWrong.B: Claude's confirmation is not evidence. It may say it covered everything even when an item is missing or a detail is wrong.
whyWrong.C: A score does not tell you which item is missing or whether the start date is correct, so you would still have to do the check yourself.

questions.mindset: Check the output against the request, one requirement at a time.

questions.stem: A marketing analyst uploads a CSV of last quarter's campaign spend and asks Claude for a short summary for the finance team. Claude reports total spend of $412,600 and says paid social was 'about 38% of spend'. The analyst plans to paste both figures into a budget review deck. Which action gives the MOST trustworthy check of these numbers for the least effort?

options.text: Recompute the total and the paid-social share from the CSV (one SUM and one division), or have Claude run the calculation and show its working.
Ask Claude 'Are you sure about these numbers?' and use both figures in the deck if it confirms them without changing anything.
Compare both figures with last quarter's deck and accept them if they fall within roughly the same range as the previous quarter.
Run the same prompt in a fresh conversation and use the figures in the deck only if the two conversations return matching answers.

questions.explanation: Numbers that are going to finance should be **recomputed from the source data**, not taken on trust. A spreadsheet SUM and one division take a minute and settle the question. Claude can also analyze an uploaded CSV by running code, and when it shows the calculation you can see exactly which rows and columns it used. Both methods check the figures against the data rather than against more model text.

whyWrong.B: Asking 'are you sure?' gets you a reply, not a calculation. Claude may confirm a wrong figure, or change a right one just because it was asked.
whyWrong.C: Being close to last quarter only shows the numbers are plausible. A real change in spending, or an error that happens to land near last quarter's figure, would get past this check.
whyWrong.D: Two runs that agree can still share the same mistake, such as reading the wrong column. Agreement between outputs is weaker evidence than a direct calculation on the file.

questions.mindset: Recompute important numbers from the source data; don't ask the model to vouch for them.

questions.stem: A project manager pastes in a 90-minute meeting transcript and asks Claude to list the action items, each with an owner and a due date. Claude returns 14 items. The list goes to the whole team in 10 minutes, and a wrong owner or deadline would cause confusion. What is the MOST efficient way to check the list for accuracy?

options.text: Ask Claude to reformat the list as a table with columns for item, owner and date, since a table makes errors easier to spot.
Send the list to the whole team now and ask each person to reply if any item assigned to them names the wrong owner or date.
Ask Claude to add the transcript line supporting each owner and date, then check those lines and flag any item without one.
Ask Claude to drop any item it is less than 90% confident about, then send the shorter and more reliable list to the team.

questions.explanation: Asking Claude to back each claim with a **direct quote from the source** makes the list auditable. The project manager no longer has to re-read 90 minutes of transcript. She only checks 14 short quotes against the items they support. An item with no supporting quote, or with a quote that doesn't actually assign that owner or date, is exactly the kind of invented detail she needs to catch. Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations recommends this pattern.

whyWrong.A: A table changes how the list looks, not whether it is right. A wrong owner is just as wrong in a neat column.
whyWrong.B: This sends unchecked errors to the whole team and relies on people noticing them. Silence does not mean an item is correct, and the confusion has already started.
whyWrong.D: Self-rated confidence is not a reliable sign of accuracy. Dropping items could also remove real action items, so the list ends up less complete as well as unchecked.

questions.mindset: Make each claim traceable to the source, then check the trace.

questions.stem: An operations lead uses Claude to answer staff questions about the company's travel expense policy, with the policy PDF attached. One answer says employees can claim a daily meal allowance 'in line with standard government rates.' The lead can find no mention of government rates anywhere in the policy. What should she do to make answers like this accurate from now on?

options.text: Accept the answer as it stands, since government meal rates are a widely used benchmark that Claude probably knows well enough.
Instruct Claude to answer only from the attached policy, quote the section used, and flag questions the policy doesn't cover.
Upload several other companies' travel policies too, so Claude has more examples of how meal allowances usually work.
Switch to the most capable model, which will be less likely to add general knowledge when a document is attached.

questions.explanation: Claude has mixed general knowledge into an answer that should come only from the company's policy. That makes the answer inaccurate for this purpose even if government rates are a real thing. The fix is to **restrict Claude to the supplied document**, ask it to quote the section it relies on so each answer can be checked, and give it explicit permission to say the policy is silent. The lead should also correct the answer staff have already seen.

whyWrong.A: Staff will act on this answer as company policy. A benchmark the policy never mentions is an invented rule, however reasonable it sounds.
whyWrong.C: Adding other companies' rules gives Claude more outside material to blend in, which makes this kind of error more likely, not less.
whyWrong.D: A more capable model can still fill gaps from general knowledge. The problem is solved by the instruction and by checking quotes, not by model size.

questions.mindset: When the answer must come from your documents, say so and make Claude show where it found it.

questions.stem: A consultant uses Claude's research mode to prepare a briefing on how three regional competitors price their service plans. The report is well organized, and every key claim has a citation. It goes to a client next week. Which TWO actions BEST check the report's accuracy? Choose TWO.

options.text: Open the cited sources for the key claims and confirm that each one exists and says what the report says it does.
Count the citations and treat the report as reliable if every paragraph has at least one source attached to it.
Ask Claude to rewrite the report in a more formal, consulting-style tone so it is ready for the client to read.
Check each source's date and confirm current prices on the competitors' own websites, since prices change often.
Run research mode again with the same question and keep whichever version of the report includes the larger number of sources.

questions.explanation: Research mode provides citations so that you can **check them**, not so that you can skip checking. Two things can go wrong. A claim can cite a real source that doesn't actually support it, or that only supports part of it, which you catch by opening the source. Or a source can be accurate but old, which matters a lot for something like pricing, and you catch that by checking dates and the competitors' current pages. Anthropic's guidance on reducing hallucinations is the same in principle: verify each claim against the underlying source before you rely on it.

whyWrong.B: Having a citation is not the same as being supported by it. A paragraph can cite a page that says something different, or nothing relevant at all.
whyWrong.C: Changing the tone does nothing for accuracy. A polished report with a wrong price is still wrong, and now it looks more convincing.
whyWrong.E: More sources do not make a report more accurate. You would still have checked none of them.

questions.mindset: Citations are an invitation to verify, not a substitute for it.

questions.stem: A communications officer asks Claude to rewrite a dense leave policy in plain language for frontline staff. The original says managers 'may approve' up to five days of unpaid leave 'subject to operational needs.' The rewrite says 'You can take up to five days of unpaid leave.' It is far easier to read and scores well on a readability tool. What is the MOST important issue to fix before it is published?

options.text: The rewrite is very short and should be expanded so frontline staff don't feel that the policy has been oversimplified.
The readability score should be confirmed with a second readability tool before this version of the policy is approved.
The rewrite should be regenerated in a warmer tone so that frontline staff feel more supported by the new leave policy.
The meaning changed: conditional manager approval became an entitlement, so check conditions and limits line by line.

questions.explanation: Simplifying is where meaning most easily drifts. 'Managers may approve, subject to operational needs' has become 'you can take', which turns a discretionary, conditional decision into a right. Staff who rely on the rewrite will expect leave the policy doesn't guarantee. When you check a rewrite, compare it with the original **line by line** for obligations (may/must/will), conditions, numbers, dates and exceptions. Readability is worth having only once the meaning is still correct.

whyWrong.A: Length is not the problem. A short rewrite is fine if it keeps the meaning, and a longer one could still contain the same error.
whyWrong.B: A second readability score measures how easy the text is to read, not whether it is right. The rewrite reads easily precisely because it dropped the condition.
whyWrong.C: A warmer tone does nothing about the change in meaning, and it makes the inaccurate promise sound more reassuring.

questions.mindset: When text is simplified, check that rights, conditions and numbers survived the rewrite.

questions.stem: A small-business owner asks Claude, with web search turned off, which of two accounting software products currently offers the cheaper plan for a five-person team. Claude answers clearly and gives specific monthly prices. What is the BEST way to treat this answer?

options.text: Treat the prices as possibly out of date and confirm them on each vendor's current pricing page before deciding.
Trust the prices as given, since Claude provided exact figures for each product rather than vague or rounded ranges.
Ask Claude how confident it is in the prices, and accept the figures if it says its confidence is high.
Ask Claude the same question again in a new conversation, then average the two sets of prices into one figure.

questions.explanation: Without web search, Claude answers from its training data, which has a cutoff date and may not reflect current prices. Prices change often, so a specific-looking figure can be outdated or simply wrong. For anything **current**, such as prices, plans, people in roles or recent events, confirm with the live, authoritative source before you decide.

whyWrong.B: Exact figures can make an answer look more reliable than it is. Specific details are exactly where outdated or invented information hides.
whyWrong.C: Self-reported confidence is not evidence. Claude cannot know about price changes made after its training data was collected.
whyWrong.D: Averaging two possibly outdated answers gives you a number that may match neither the old price nor the current one.

questions.mindset: For anything current, check the live source; training data has a cutoff.

questions.stem: A nonprofit's development officer has 20 minutes to check a Claude-drafted donor newsletter before it goes to 8,000 supporters. The draft contains a thank-you paragraph, a general description of the charity's mission, a statistic that 'our programs reached 12,400 families last year', a quote attributed to the board chair, and a closing appeal to donate. With limited time, which TWO parts should she verify first? Choose TWO.

options.text: The general description of the mission, since it sets the tone for the rest of the newsletter.
The 12,400 families statistic, checked against the annual report or the program's own records.
The thank-you paragraph, since donors are sensitive to how gratitude is expressed to them.
The closing appeal, checking that it is persuasive enough to work as an end-of-year fundraising ask.
The board chair's quote, confirming the chair actually said these words or approves them.

questions.explanation: When time is short, verify the **specific factual claims** first, because that is where fabrication is most likely and where an error does the most damage. An exact statistic and a quote attributed to a real, named person both look authoritative, both can be fabricated, and both are embarrassing to correct once 8,000 people have read them. The general and persuasive sections are worth editing too, but they carry little factual risk.

whyWrong.A: A general description of the mission is low-risk and easy to fix later. Usually it is a matter of wording, not a factual claim.
whyWrong.C: Tone in a thank-you paragraph matters, but it is an editing question, not an accuracy risk. Nothing in it can be proved false.
whyWrong.D: How persuasive the appeal is affects quality, not accuracy. Polishing it before checking the facts gets the priorities backwards.

questions.mindset: Check specifics first: numbers, names, dates and quotes are where errors hide and hurt most.

questions.stem: A training coordinator asks Claude for a brief history of a workplace safety regulation for a course handout. She regenerates the answer to get a shorter version and notices that the year the regulation took effect is different in the two versions. The rest of the content looks much the same. What is the MOST appropriate conclusion and next step?

options.text: Use the year from the more detailed version, since longer answers usually reflect more careful reasoning about dates.
Regenerate the answer a third time and use whichever year appears in two of the three versions as the correct date.
Treat the mismatch as a warning and confirm the year, and the handout's other specifics, from an official source.
Remove the year from the handout and keep everything else, since only the year changed between the two versions.

questions.explanation: When the same question gives **different facts on different runs**, that is a strong sign the model is unsure and may be inventing details. Anthropic's guidance describes comparing several outputs as a way to spot hallucinations. A mismatch is a reason to check, though, not a way to decide which answer is right. Settle the date from an authoritative source, such as the regulator's own site, and check the handout's other specific facts too, because two runs agreeing on them does not prove they are correct.

whyWrong.A: Length is not evidence. A longer answer can contain the wrong date just as easily as a shorter one.
whyWrong.B: A majority vote between model outputs is still not evidence. The model can repeat the same wrong year twice.
whyWrong.D: This hides the one problem you noticed and assumes everything else is right only because it was consistent. Consistency does not show that something is accurate.

questions.mindset: Inconsistency between runs tells you where to check; only an authoritative source tells you the answer.

questions.stem: A procurement analyst gives Claude three vendor proposals and asks for a comparison table of price, implementation time, support hours, data-hosting region and contract length. Every cell in the table is filled in. When she spot-checks, she finds that one vendor's proposal never mentions a hosting region, yet the table lists 'EU' for that vendor. What is the BEST way to fix the table and prevent the same problem?

options.text: Have Claude mark values a proposal doesn't state as 'Not stated in proposal', cite a section for each filled cell, and check those cells.
Delete the data-hosting row from the table, since it is the only row where the spot-check found a problem with the values.
Ask Claude to fill each missing value with the most likely answer based on similar vendors, and label each one as an estimate.
Keep the table as it is but add a footnote saying that the comparison was generated by AI and may contain some errors.

questions.explanation: A table with **every cell filled** should make you suspicious when the source documents are uneven. Here Claude filled a gap with a plausible value instead of reporting that the information was missing. Give it explicit permission to write 'not stated', and ask it to cite where each value came from. That makes the table both honest and checkable. A 'not stated' cell is itself useful: it tells the analyst what to ask that vendor before a decision is made.

whyWrong.B: The other rows have only been spot-checked, not verified, and hosting region may matter for the decision. Removing the row hides the problem instead of fixing it.
whyWrong.C: A label does not make a guessed hosting region useful. It is still an invented value in a document that will drive a purchasing decision.
whyWrong.D: A disclaimer does not correct an error you already know about. The reader is still shown a value that is wrong.

questions.mindset: Missing information should be reported as missing, not filled with something plausible.

questions.stem: An e-commerce coordinator uses Claude to write 60 product descriptions. Each must be under 300 characters, state the product's material as given in the supplied spec sheet, and avoid any health claims. Claude says all 60 meet the requirements. Which TWO checks BEST confirm the batch before upload? Choose TWO.

options.text: Accept Claude's statement that all 60 meet the rules, since it has already checked its own work in its reply.
Read the first five descriptions closely and approve the whole batch of 60 if those five meet all three rules.
Measure every description's length with a spreadsheet character-count formula rather than trusting Claude's claim.
Ask Claude to rewrite every description in a more engaging style so that the whole batch reads consistently.
Check a sample from across the batch against the spec sheet, and scan all 60 for wording that sounds like a health claim.

questions.explanation: Match each check to the requirement. **Length** is a mechanical rule, so measure it mechanically: a character-count formula checks all 60 in seconds and is never wrong about length. **Material accuracy** needs a comparison with the spec sheet, and a sample drawn from across the batch (not just the start) is a sensible check on a large set. **Health claims** carry regulatory risk, so every description should be scanned, not just a sample. Claude's statement that everything passes is not one of these checks.

whyWrong.A: A model's report on its own output is not verification. It can say a description is under 300 characters when it isn't.
whyWrong.B: The first five are not a representative sample. Problems often show up later in a long batch, and one risky health claim is enough to cause harm.
whyWrong.D: A consistent style has nothing to do with the three rules, and rewriting all 60 could introduce new errors you would then need to check.

questions.mindset: Use a deterministic check for mechanical rules and a source comparison for facts; never take the model's word that it complied.

questions.stem: A school principal asks Claude to draft a graduation speech. The draft opens with an inspiring line attributed to a well-known author, and the principal has never come across this quote before. What should the principal do?

options.text: Keep the quote, since a line that fits the author's known style and themes is very likely to be genuine.
Confirm in a reliable source that the author said or wrote it, and remove or replace it if not.
Ask Claude which book the quote originally comes from, and keep it if Claude can name a specific title.
Keep the line but change the attribution to 'as someone once said' to avoid any possible risk.

questions.explanation: Claude can produce quotes that sound authoritative but were never said, and putting fabricated words in a real person's mouth in public is both embarrassing and unfair to them. Before using any attributed quote, **confirm it in a reliable source**. If you can't confirm it, cut it or replace it with one you have verified.

whyWrong.A: Fitting the author's style is exactly what makes a made-up quote convincing. It is not evidence that the author said it.
whyWrong.C: A book title from Claude is more unverified output. It can be invented just as easily as the quote.
whyWrong.D: 'As someone once said' still presents the line as a real quotation. Either verify it or use it as the principal's own words without calling it a quote.

questions.mindset: Never publish an attributed quote you haven't confirmed in a reliable source.

questions.stem: A customer-service team lead exports last month's 1,200 support tickets and asks Claude to summarize the complaint themes, with counts, for a leadership meeting. Claude returns six themes, each with a count. Which TWO checks BEST confirm that the summary is accurate and complete? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence in each theme count and to drop any theme that it rates below 80 percent.
Reconcile the counts with the 1,200 tickets (allowing for tickets in more than one theme) and trace any missing ones.
Rewrite the summary in a short executive style so the leadership team can read the whole thing in under two minutes.
Read a sample of tickets from each theme, plus some that fit no theme, to confirm grouping and spot missed themes.
Run the summary again with the most capable model available, and replace the original counts with that model's counts.

questions.explanation: Two checks cover the two risks. **Reconciling counts** with the source total catches tickets that were dropped or double-counted, which is a completeness and accuracy check on the numbers. **Sampling tickets** within each theme shows whether the grouping is right, and reading tickets that fit no theme shows whether a real issue (a new product defect, say) has been left out. Leadership will make decisions from this summary, so both checks are worth the effort.

whyWrong.A: Self-rated confidence is not a reliable sign of accuracy, and dropping themes can remove real issues. That makes the summary less complete, not more.
whyWrong.C: A shorter summary is easier to read but no more accurate. It can also hide the gaps you were supposed to find.
whyWrong.E: A more capable model gives you a different set of unchecked counts. Swapping one for the other verifies nothing against the tickets.

questions.mindset: Reconcile totals against the source and sample the underlying records to check both accuracy and coverage.

questions.stem: A finance assistant asks Claude to convert a 12-page scanned PDF of supplier invoices into a spreadsheet with one row per invoice. The result has 214 rows and looks clean. The spreadsheet will be used to pay suppliers. What is the MOST reliable check before it is used?

options.text: Ask Claude to confirm that it extracted every invoice and read every amount correctly from the scanned pages.
Check that the file opens without errors and that every column has the right heading and number formatting.
Have Claude convert the PDF again and use the file only if both versions have exactly the same number of rows.
Reconcile the invoice count and total with the PDF or supplier statements, and spot-check rows against the scan.

questions.explanation: Payments depend on this data, so check it **against the original**, in two ways. Reconciling the count and the grand total against an independent figure (totals printed in the PDF, or the supplier statements) catches missing, duplicated or badly misread rows. Spot-checking individual rows, especially where the scan is blurry or handwritten, catches errors that cancel out in the totals or are too small to notice there. A clean-looking file proves only that the formatting worked.

whyWrong.A: Claude's confirmation is not evidence. It cannot reliably vouch for its own reading of a blurry scan.
whyWrong.B: This checks the formatting, not the content. A well-formatted file can still contain a misread amount or skip an invoice.
whyWrong.C: Getting the same row count twice does not show the amounts are right, and both runs can misread the same unclear digits.

questions.mindset: Clean-looking output proves formatting, not accuracy; reconcile against an independent total and spot-check the source.
